segments.line: Day four. Sixteen hundred.
And you are starving. You
eat breakfast. Then a second breakfast. Then Ellie's breakfast.
By lunch, you've eaten more than your whole family. And you're still hungry.
Here's why. Your brain is only about two percent of your body's weight.
But it burns about twenty percent of your energy.
Even when you're asleep, it's the hungriest thing you own.
Your whole body, sitting still, runs on about eighty watts. Twenty of those go to your brain.
That's like a light bulb burning inside your head. All day. Every day.
Now that brain is doing sixteen times the work. Every morning, it needs more fuel.
And everything that burns fuel makes heat.
There's a second catch, too. Talking to people starts to feel like watching a video at quarter speed. You know how every sentence ends before it's halfway out.
Mo tells you a joke, and you see the punchline in his face before he says it. You laugh anyway.
A second too late. And for the first time in your life, you feel lonely in a room full of people.
Day five. Three thousand two hundred.
You wake up with your pillow soaked. Mom puts a hand on your forehead and pulls it back fast. The
thermometer says thirty- nine point four.
Doctors say that at forty degrees, your body starts to break down. That's heatstroke. Proteins in your brain begin to stop working.
And your temperature is rising a little more every morning.
That's the other problem with doubling. It feels slow, then it isn't. If you keep going like this, by day ten your IQ would be over a hundred thousand. By day
thirty, a hundred billion.
But you won't make it to day thirty. You do
the math lying on the bathroom floor, with a bag of frozen peas on your head. At this rate, your brain cooks in three days.
